title: Week 110 · Lesson 134: Pediatric Vomiting, Diarrhea, Dehydration & Abdominal Pain — FNP-Level Assessment and Triage
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 110 — Lesson 134: Pediatric Vomiting, Diarrhea, Dehydration & Abdominal Pain

FNP-level goal: Distinguish uncomplicated gastroenteritis from dehydration, obstruction, surgical abdomen, metabolic disease, infection, and torsion; use age-specific history and examination to guide oral rehydration, testing, and disposition; and recognize when vomiting or abdominal pain requires immediate emergency or surgical evaluation.

Learning Objectives

  • Estimate dehydration severity from integrated history, vital signs, perfusion, mental status, mucosa, tears, urine, and weight.
  • Use oral rehydration safely for appropriate children and recognize failure criteria.
  • Differentiate gastroenteritis from dangerous vomiting and abdominal-pain patterns by age.
  • Select urine, stool, blood, imaging, and pregnancy testing only when they answer a clinical question.
  • Provide explicit feeding, infection-control, medication, and return precautions.

Part 1 — Start With Stability

Before deciding that a child has a stomach virus, assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion, and hydration. Tachycardia, hypotension, delayed capillary refill, weak pulses, cool extremities, lethargy, altered consciousness, severe pain, rigid abdomen, or inability to protect the airway requires urgent stabilization.

Children can maintain blood pressure until late shock. Normal blood pressure does not exclude clinically important dehydration. Compare current and prior weight when reliable; percent weight loss is one of the strongest objective measures of fluid deficit.

Part 2 — Characterize Vomiting Precisely

Ask onset, frequency, force, color, blood, relation to feeds, pain, distention, stool, urine, fever, headache, trauma, ingestion, polyuria, weight change, sick contacts, travel, food, medications, cannabis exposure in adolescents, pregnancy possibility, and prior surgery. Caregivers may call any yellow-green material bile; clarify whether emesis is truly dark green.

Bilious emesis, hematemesis with instability, persistent projectile vomiting in a young infant, vomiting with neurologic change, severe headache, distended or rigid abdomen, focal peritonitis, suspected ingestion, or testicular or ovarian torsion symptoms is not routine gastroenteritis.

Part 3 — Characterize Diarrhea

Clarify frequency, volume, blood, mucus, duration, fever, pain, nocturnal stool, recent antibiotics, travel, water, reptiles, daycare, sick contacts, immune status, and baseline stool pattern. Acute watery diarrhea with vomiting and household spread often supports viral gastroenteritis, but blood, severe pain, toxic appearance, prolonged course, or high-risk host factors change the differential.

Infants and toddlers can dehydrate quickly. Adolescents may underreport laxative use, eating disorder behavior, substance use, or pregnancy; confidential history can be essential.

Part 4 — Estimate Dehydration as a Pattern

No single sign is sufficient. Integrate intake, losses, urine, thirst, behavior, tears, mucous membranes, eyes, fontanelle when relevant, skin, heart rate, respiratory pattern, pulses, capillary refill, extremity temperature, and weight change. Mild dehydration may show thirst and reduced urine; moderate disease adds dry mucosa, reduced tears, tachycardia, decreased activity, or delayed refill; severe dehydration may produce lethargy, weak pulses, poor perfusion, deep breathing, and shock.

Hypernatremic dehydration may preserve skin turgor and produce neurologic irritability; do not let one apparently normal sign override the whole picture.

Part 5 — Oral Rehydration Therapy

Oral rehydration solution uses balanced glucose and electrolytes to enhance intestinal sodium and water absorption. For a stable child with mild to moderate dehydration and no surgical concern, give small, frequent measured amounts, increasing as tolerated. Continue breastfeeding and resume an age-appropriate diet as rehydration proceeds. Replace ongoing stool and emesis losses according to age and local protocol.

Juice, soda, sports drinks, and overly concentrated homemade fluids can worsen osmotic diarrhea or create electrolyte problems. Never dilute formula to treat dehydration. If vomiting interrupts oral rehydration, pause briefly and restart with smaller volumes; selected children may benefit from clinician-directed antiemetic support.

Part 6 — When Oral Rehydration Is Not Enough

Escalate when shock, severe dehydration, altered mental status, ileus or obstruction, bilious emesis, uncontrolled losses, unsafe airway, severe electrolyte concern, or repeated failure of supervised oral challenge occurs. A nasogastric rehydration pathway may be appropriate in selected monitored children; IV fluids are needed for instability or when enteral rehydration is unsafe or unsuccessful.

Reassess after treatment: heart rate, perfusion, mental status, urine, ability to drink, vomiting, pain, and caregiver capacity. A successful sip in clinic is not sufficient if the child cannot meet ongoing needs at home.

Part 7 — Acute Gastroenteritis Management

Most uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis is treated with oral rehydration, continued nutrition, hygiene, and time. Routine antibiotics are not indicated and may worsen some infections or promote resistance. Antimotility agents can be harmful in young children or invasive disease and should not be routine.

Probiotics have strain-specific and condition-specific evidence; do not treat them as interchangeable. Provide precise guidance on fluids, feeding, urine goals, handwashing, diaper hygiene, and when the child can return to childcare under local policy.

Part 8 — Stool and Blood Testing

Stool testing is most useful for bloody diarrhea, severe disease, prolonged symptoms, outbreak or public-health concern, recent antibiotics, travel, immune compromise, or when a result will change treatment. Avoid broad panels that may detect colonization without explaining illness.

Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, acid-base assessment, or other labs are appropriate with severe dehydration, altered mental status, unusual breathing, prolonged losses, metabolic concern, or IV treatment. A bedside glucose can rapidly identify hypoglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis.

Part 9 — Dangerous Infant Vomiting

Pyloric stenosis classically causes progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting in an early infant, hunger after vomiting, and dehydration; ultrasound supports diagnosis. Bilious vomiting suggests obstruction distal to the ampulla and demands urgent evaluation for malrotation with volvulus or other obstruction. Do not delay because the abdomen initially feels soft.

Also consider sepsis, UTI, cow's-milk protein-related disease, metabolic disorder, increased intracranial pressure, overfeeding, and physiologic reflux. Poor weight gain, feeding refusal, apnea, bleeding, or neurologic abnormality argues against simple reflux.

Part 10 — Abdominal Pain by Age and Pattern

Young children may localize poorly. Ask timing, migration, episodic versus constant pattern, relation to food or stool, fever, vomiting sequence, urinary and genital symptoms, bleeding, trauma, and gait. Observe movement: a child with peritonitis may avoid walking or bumps, while a child with colicky pain may draw up the legs between quiet intervals.

Differential includes constipation, gastroenteritis, UTI, appendicitis, intussusception, obstruction, hernia, pneumonia, streptococcal infection, DKA, IgA vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease, migraine, functional pain, and gynecologic or testicular disease.

Part 11 — Appendicitis

Appendicitis may begin with vague periumbilical pain followed by migration to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea or vomiting, fever, and pain with movement, but young children and pregnancy can present atypically. The sequence of pain before vomiting may support appendicitis but is not definitive.

Use serial examination, age-appropriate decision support, laboratory testing, and ultrasound-first imaging when appropriate. Do not allow a low-risk score to override peritonitis or a worsening trajectory.

Part 12 — Intussusception and Torsion

Intussusception often causes episodic severe pain, pallor, vomiting, and lethargy; currant-jelly stool is a late and inconsistent finding. A child may look well between episodes. Ultrasound supports diagnosis and urgent reduction may be needed.

Testicular torsion can present as abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting, especially in adolescents who are reluctant to mention genital symptoms. Ovarian torsion causes sudden pelvic or lower-abdominal pain, often with nausea and vomiting. Both are time-sensitive emergencies; include a respectful genital or pelvic history and indicated examination.

Part 13 — Metabolic and Extra-Abdominal Mimics

DKA may present with abdominal pain, vomiting, dehydration, polyuria, weight loss, deep breathing, and altered mental status. Pneumonia, especially lower-lobe disease, can cause abdominal pain. Head injury, meningitis, toxic ingestion, pregnancy, and eating disorders may also present with vomiting.

A narrow gastrointestinal label is unsafe when vital signs, breathing, neurologic status, or history point elsewhere.

Part 14 — Disposition and Follow-Up

Outpatient care requires improving hydration, successful oral intake, no surgical or metabolic red flags, manageable losses, reliable caregivers, and explicit follow-up. Same-day reassessment is appropriate for persistent vomiting, declining urine, worsening pain, blood in stool, prolonged fever, uncertain diagnosis, or failure to improve.

Emergency evaluation is required for shock, altered consciousness, bilious vomiting, rigid or peritoneal abdomen, severe localized or episodic pain with lethargy, GI bleeding with instability, suspected torsion, DKA, severe dehydration, or inability to maintain hydration.

Clinical Case 1 — Oral Rehydration Candidate

A two-year-old with watery diarrhea and several episodes of nonbilious emesis is alert, mildly tachycardic, has dry mucosa, and still urinates. The abdomen is soft without focal pain. The FNP supervises small frequent oral rehydration, reassesses physiology and intake, continues age-appropriate nutrition, and provides precise failure criteria.

Clinical Case 2 — Projectile Is Not Bilious

A five-week-old has progressively forceful nonbilious vomiting after feeds, seems hungry afterward, and is losing weight. The FNP arranges urgent evaluation for pyloric stenosis and dehydration rather than diagnosing reflux or changing formula repeatedly.

Clinical Case 3 — Well Between Episodes

An 18-month-old has sudden recurrent episodes of screaming and drawing up the legs, pallor, vomiting, and sleepiness between episodes. The FNP recognizes possible intussusception and sends the child for emergency imaging and treatment without waiting for bloody stool.

FNP High-Yield Framework: ABDOMEN

  1. A — Assess stability: perfusion, mental status, glucose, hydration, pain severity.
  2. B — Bilious, blood, or ballistic: green emesis, GI bleeding, progressive projectile vomiting.
  3. D — Define losses and intake: frequency, urine, weight change, oral challenge.
  4. O — Observe the pattern: focal, migratory, episodic, peritoneal, genital, neurologic.
  5. M — Match tests to risk: urine, stool, labs, ultrasound, pregnancy testing when indicated.
  6. E — Enterally rehydrate when safe: balanced solution, small frequent volumes, continued nutrition.
  7. N — Name failure and next steps: reassessment time, emergency signs, responsible clinician.

Take-Home Summary

The safest pediatric gastrointestinal assessment begins with perfusion and hydration, then uses age and symptom pattern to separate self-limited disease from obstruction, appendicitis, intussusception, torsion, DKA, and extra-abdominal illness. Oral rehydration is active treatment, but only when the airway, abdomen, mental status, and follow-up are safe.

Educational note: Follow current pediatric rehydration, infectious-disease, imaging, and emergency protocols. Shock, altered mental status, bilious vomiting, severe dehydration, peritoneal findings, suspected torsion, GI bleeding with instability, DKA, or inability to hydrate requires urgent evaluation.
